A pretty enjoyable game about facing one's trauma and not turning away from it. I can clearly see the inspiration drawn from VNs and ADVs (Zero Escape, Danganronpa, Ace Attorney, Needy Girl Overdose), and it's very cute seeing the gameplay from them incorporated here. I liked watching the cast bond and also enjoyed seeing the story unfold. It's a colorful cast of characters! 

I just finished the game and the ending made me tear up. It's lovely! I loved the message of it. 

I must admit, however, the English translation really is rough. There's many typos, spaces missing, odd line breaks, and a lot of stuff sounds stilted. That said, I did see that the English script is being looked over to be reworked. I'm very happy about that!

This game isn't one I would say blew me out of the water, but I still had a good time with it. I look forward to seeing what other games you guys make in the future!

Type-Noise is an escape game and visual novel hybrid (a la Zero Escape) that has mostly fun puzzles and a good, but somewhat disjointed story.

Soto Ochibana awakens in a sewer with a girl his age named Zena Yugamizora. After a quick escape sequence, they exit to a strange version of Shibuya where everyone, except for four other teens, seems to be a mindless drone. After discovering that all of them have no memory of how or why they got there, and exploring the city for a bit, they are chased away by those drone-like people and forced to hide in either an arcade or a karaoke bar, depending on your choice.

As Soto and Co make their way through the city, he and his current partner find themselves in a series of escape rooms relating to the latter. As they investigate the escape rooms for a means of escape, they also find "Noise" that represents their past trauma. After collecting enough pieces of Noise, Soto and his partner see a scene that reveals a key aspect of the latter's trauma.

From a gameplay perspective, the escape rooms were pretty great. There is a nice variety of puzzles (even an homage to Ace Attorney at one point), and they do a good job of showcasing their respective character's personality and backstory. There are also some UI elements that make the puzzles not so much of a hassle as they can be in other games. There's always an objective in the top left corner suggesting what you should do next, like "Combine Item X with something else," or "Solve this area"—nothing to intrusive, but enough to make it so you're not totally lost. (Although, even without that, most of the puzzles are structured in such a way that it's usually intuitive what to do next.) Some of the gameplay elements didn't click with me, especially the debate segments, but overall, they were fun.

The story, which gives each character a turn in the spotlight, was not as consistent, though. Some of the characters, like Itsuki and Hiyori, had interesting, emotionally resonant stories focusing on the pressure of being a high academic achiever and the negative aspects of content creation, respectively, while others, like Honoka and especially Kaito, were merely decent. Also, the other four characters' stories have only a loose connection to Zena and Soto's stories, which are the real highlight of the story, but you have to see all four other characters' stories first. Even so, while I did enjoy Soto's story, at times, it felt overly straightforward—even preachy, sometimes—in its messaging.

Overall, while Type Noise kills it on the escape-room gameplay aspect, the story is only alright. The escape puzzles are a large portion of the game, though, so if that kind of gameplay is your jam, Type Noise is an easy recommendation, despite its mixed-quality story.

6/10

[h2]Review for [b]Type-NOISE: Shonen Shojo[/b] - Positive (After 100% Achievements and All Endings)[/h2]

[i]Overall, this is a solid, enjoyable game that kept me engaged from start to finish. It's a great fit for fans of visual novels with an anime art style blended with puzzle elements—definitely recommend it if that sounds like your jam.[/i]

[h3][b]* Pros:[/b][/h3]
 [i]- Performance:[/i] Runs super smooth without any issues or crashes; it's playable and reliable all the way through.
 [i] - Graphics: [/i] The 2D anime art style is gorgeous and really brings the world to life—big thumbs up.
 [i] - Puzzle Gameplay (Point-and-Click Mechanics) [/i]: Pretty solid overall; most puzzles aren't overly brain-busting, and the hint system is helpful even if you're not a puzzle pro like me.
 [i] - Story Overall:[/i] The narrative pacing is good, building curiosity effectively. Each character has their own compelling backstory without getting overshadowed by the protagonist, which motivated me to explore other characters and chase different endings.
 [i] BGM and SFX:[/i] Decent and fitting; they enhance the atmosphere without distracting.

[h3][b]* Cons and Suggestions for Improvement:[/b][/h3]
 - It sometimes feels more like a collection of mini-puzzle games stitched together rather than a seamless whole.
 - You might not grasp the full story unless you dive deep into all the side characters and paths—which is rewarding but could be clearer.
 - Playing in [i]English[/i], I noticed some minor [i]spelling errors[/i] in the translation; a quick proofread would polish it up.
 - The [i]font size[/i] in dialogues feels a bit too small for my taste — adding an option to adjust font size would be a nice accessibility tweak.
 - [i]When replaying a chapter[/i] [b](especially ones with branching choices)[/b], it'd be great to jump straight to the decision points instead of having to skip through all the preceding dialogue. This would save a ton of time for achievement hunters.

[i]-> In summary, it's a fun, worthwhile playthrough that's perfect for anyone into anime-inspired visual novels with light puzzles. With a few refinements, it could be even better.[/i]

The translation into English is extremely poor, unfortunately. The game concept is interesting and I enjoyed the puzzle stuff I got to try, but I can't recommend this as is.

The font's also incredibly small. I was able to comfortably read it on a 32" monitor at my Desk, but the Steam Deck was nothing but eye-strain inducing.

This game wants to talk about love, scandal, rape, public judgment, the value of negative memories, and more, but it feels too scattershot to really handle any of those topics. I think the devs should have chosen one thing to write in depth about.
